title: Comparing texts
examples: How can I show the difference between two poems?
What is the best way to compare two different articles?
When I compare texts, should I focus on the topic or the style?

explain.say: Today we are learning to compare texts effectively for your writing.
First we look for similarities in the main ideas presented by both texts.
Next we examine the differences in the core ideas or arguments.
We must also compare the methods the writers use to make their points.
For example, one text might use emotional language while the other uses facts.
In everyday life, you compare two job adverts to see which is better for you.

faq.q: Should I summarize the texts first before comparing them?
faq.a: Yes, you should understand each text separately first. This helps you find the specific points to compare later. You could also ask, 'Do I need to read them twice?' or 'Is summarizing a necessary first step?'
asks: Do I need to summarize first?
Is summarizing a necessary first step?

faq.q: When comparing ideas, should I just list the similarities and differences?
faq.a: No, you need to analyze why they are similar or different. Explain the effect of the difference. You might also ask, 'Should I just list them?' or 'How do I explain the difference?'
asks: How do I explain the difference?

faq.q: Is comparing methods the same as comparing ideas?
faq.a: No, methods are how the writer writes, while ideas are what the writer says. For example, using vivid imagery is a method. You could also ask, 'Are methods and ideas the same thing?' or 'What is the difference between 'how' and 'what'?'
asks: Are methods and ideas the same thing?
What is the difference between 'how' and 'what'?
Are methods and ideas the same?

faq.q: If the texts are about the same topic, do I still need to compare them?
faq.a: Yes, even if the topic is the same, the approach or attitude can differ greatly. You should always look for the angle taken. You could ask, 'Does the topic matter?' or 'Can they be on the same topic?'
asks: Can they be on the same topic?
Do I still need to compare them?

faq.q: How do I make sure my comparison is balanced?
faq.a: A balanced comparison gives equal attention to both texts' strengths and weaknesses. Do not favour one text over the other in your writing. You could also ask, 'How do I be fair?', or 'Should I spend equal time on both?'
asks: Should I spend equal time on both?
How do I make it balanced?

facts: Comparison requires identifying both common ground and points of contrast.
Analyzing methods involves looking at language devices like metaphor or tone.
Similarities can be found in the central theme, while differences might be in the evidence used.
When comparing, always link the similarity or difference back to the writer's purpose.

quiz.say: Text A suggests change is slow, while Text B demands immediate action. This is a difference in:

options.show: The urgency of the required action.
options.say: The urgency of the required action.

quiz.why: This focuses on the core message or viewpoint, which is an idea.

wrong.0: Vocabulary is part of the language, but the idea is the message conveyed.
wrong.2: This describes the writing style, which is a method, not the idea itself.
wrong.3: Paragraph length is a structural choice, not a point of comparison.

quiz.say: Both texts use vivid descriptions of nature, but Text A focuses on beauty, and Text B focuses on decay. This is a comparison of:

options.show: The focus of their descriptive methods.
options.say: The focus of their descriptive methods.

quiz.why: You are comparing how they use description, which is a method.

wrong.1: This ignores the difference in focus (beauty versus decay).
wrong.2: This only identifies the topic, not the difference in approach.
wrong.3: While both use it, this option fails to capture the contrasting focus within that method.

quiz.say: Text A argues for policy change using statistics, and Text B argues for personal change using emotional appeals. This shows a difference in:

options.show: Their shared belief in human capability.
options.say: Their shared belief in human capability.

quiz.why: The difference lies in the tools used to persuade, which are the methods.

wrong.0: This is too general and misses the specific contrast between data and emotion.
wrong.2: This ignores the fundamental difference in how they try to convince the reader.
wrong.3: The issue's seriousness is assumed; the comparison must focus on the writing difference.
